standard_text: Understand that a function assigns to each x-value (independent variable) exactly one y-value (dependent variable), and that the graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs (x, y); determine whether a relation (set of ordered pairs, table, mapping, or graph) is a function.

progression.narrative:
Standard 8.AF.3 asks students to do two things: UNDERSTAND what a function is -- a rule that assigns to each input (x, the independent variable) exactly one output (y, the dependent variable) -- and DETERMINE whether a given relation is a function, no matter how it is shown (a set of ordered pairs, a table, a mapping, or a graph). The whole standard turns on one asymmetric rule: an input may not point to two different outputs, but two different inputs ARE allowed to share the same output. Nearly every student mistake is a failure to keep that asymmetry straight -- they disqualify a relation because an OUTPUT repeats, when only a repeated INPUT paired with different outputs breaks the rule.

So the arc starts by naming the parts: which number is the input (independent variable, the x, first in the pair) and which is the output (dependent variable, the y, second in the pair). Then students state the definition precisely -- each input has exactly one output -- and learn to test it. They apply that test first to a set of ordered pairs (scan for a repeated x paired with a different y), then to a table or mapping (the same scan in a new format), then to a graph (the vertical line test, which is just 'does any single x-value sit under two points'). The capstone puts the relation in a real-world story and asks students not only to decide but to justify -- and to critique a classmate who judged by the output instead of the input. The through-line we keep naming: a function is a one-way promise from each input to a single output; repeated outputs are fine, a repeated input with different outputs is not.

steps.rationale: Before you can test a relation you must know which number is the input (independent variable) and which is the output (dependent variable). This settles the vocabulary the whole standard leans on and where the input/output confusion first appears.
State the definition precisely -- each input has exactly one output -- and reject the reversed version (each output has one input). The definition is the tool every later determination applies.

Apply the definition to a set of ordered pairs: scan for a repeated x-value paired with different y-values. This is the core grade-level determination and where the 'repeated output' misconception is corrected.
Run the same input-uniqueness test on a table or mapping. A new representation with the identical logic forces the criterion to transfer beyond ordered-pair notation.

Because the graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs (x, y), testing a graph is the vertical line test -- does any single x sit under two points. This extends the criterion to the visual representation named in the standard.

The above-grade synthesis: decide whether a real-world relation is a function, justify with the definition, and critique a classmate who judged by a repeated output. Proves students own the asymmetric rule, not just a procedure.

skills.name: Identify the x-value and y-value within an ordered pair

prerequisite_skill.description: Read an ordered pair (x, y): the first number is x, the second is y.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In the ordered pair (7, 2), which number is the x-value?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is written (x, y): the FIRST number is always the x-value, the SECOND is always the y-value. The order is fixed and never changes. Watch (7, 2): the x-value is 7 (first), the y-value is 2 (second). If I flip them I get a different point, so I read left to right: x first, y second.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the pair -- reads the second number as x and the first as y
canonical_error.example: For (7, 2) says the x-value is 2 and the y-value is 7
canonical_error.why: The student does not hold the fixed order (x first, y second) and swaps the coordinates. The first slot is always x, the horizontal/input value.

skills.item_template: A single ordered pair. Student names its x-value and y-value. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: In the ordered pair (7, 2), what is the x-value?
In the ordered pair (7, 2), what is the y-value?
In the ordered pair (-3, 5), what is the x-value?
In the ordered pair (0, 9), what is the y-value?
Which number comes first in an ordered pair, the x-value or the y-value?
sample_items.answer: The x-value

redirect_script.stop: Which slot is the x -- first or second?
redirect_script.prompt: An ordered pair is (x, y): the FIRST number is x, the second is y. Point to the first number and say 'x', the second and say 'y'.
redirect_script.praise: You read the first number as x and the second as y -- that's the order that never changes.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers written (x, y) that name a single point or input-output pair.
The first number in an ordered pair; the input.
The second number in an ordered pair; the output.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Name the x-value and y-value of (5, 8).'
Which number is first? What is that number always called?
First is 5, so x = 5. Second is 8, so y = 8. x first, y second.
If a student says x = 8, ask 'which number did you WRITE first when you made the pair?'
Your turn: name the x-value and y-value of (2, 6).

skills.name: Read a table or mapping as a set of ordered pairs (x, y)

prerequisite_skill.description: Pair each input with its output to turn a table or mapping into ordered pairs (x, y).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A table shows x = 3 with y = 8 in the same row. Write that as an ordered pair.

skills.i_do_script: A table and a mapping hold the same information as a set of ordered pairs -- I just pair each input with the output next to it. Watch a table with rows x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 5, 6: the first row is (1, 4), the second (2, 5), the third (3, 6). A mapping arrow from 2 to 7 is just the pair (2, 7): the value the arrow starts at is x, the value it points to is y.

canonical_error.pattern: Pairs values across rows or reverses input and output when reading a table
canonical_error.example: From a row x = 3, y = 8 writes (8, 3), or pairs the x from one row with the y from the next
canonical_error.why: The student loses the row-by-row pairing or the input-first order. Each ordered pair comes from ONE row: (input, output).

skills.item_template: A small table or mapping. Student writes the ordered pairs. Short response.

sample_items.stem: A table row shows x = 3 and y = 8. Write it as an ordered pair.
Write the ordered pairs for this table.
A mapping shows an arrow from 2 to 7. Write it as an ordered pair (input, output).
Write the ordered pairs for this table.

redirect_script.stop: Do those two numbers share a row?
redirect_script.prompt: Take ONE row at a time. The x in that row and the y in that same row make one pair: (x, y). Slide your finger across a single row.
redirect_script.praise: You kept each pair to one row, input first -- that's the table as ordered pairs.

vocabulary.definition: Any set of ordered pairs; it can be shown as a list, a table, a mapping, or a graph.
A diagram with arrows from each input to its output(s).
Input and output values lined up in rows or columns.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a table: x = 2, 5 and y = 9, 1.
Read across the first row -- what x goes with what y?
Row one is (2, 9); row two is (5, 1). Each pair comes from one row, input first.
If a student writes (9, 2), ask 'which value is the input in that row?'
Your turn: write the ordered pairs for x = 1, 3 and y = 6, 8.

skills.name: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a relation
skills.i_do_script: The independent variable is the INPUT -- the x-value, the first number in each ordered pair, the quantity you choose or control. The dependent variable is the OUTPUT -- the y-value, the second number, the quantity that responds. Watch the set {(3, -5), (-2, 4), (7, 1)}: the independent variables (x-values) are 3, -2, and 7, the first number in each pair. The dependent variables (y-values) are -5, 4, and 1. Input first, output second, every time.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the roles -- names the y-value (output) as the independent variable
canonical_error.example: For (3, -5) calls -5 the independent variable instead of 3
canonical_error.why: The student forgets the independent variable is the input (the x, the first coordinate you control) and the dependent variable is the output (the y, the second coordinate that responds).

skills.item_template: A set of ordered pairs, a table, or a labeled context. Student selects the independent or dependent variables. Multi-select / short response.

sample_items.stem: In the set {(3, -5), (-2, 4), (7, 1)}, list all the independent variables (x-values).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Independent = x = first coordinate. -5, 4, 1 are the dependent (y) values.

sample_items.stem: In the ordered pair (6, 11), which value is the dependent variable?
sample_items.answer: 11 (the y-value / output)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Dependent = output = y = second coordinate. 6 is the independent value.

sample_items.stem: A table has an 'Hours worked' column and a 'Pay earned' column. Which is the independent variable?
sample_items.answer: Hours worked (the input)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Pay depends on hours, so hours is the independent variable and pay is dependent.

sample_items.stem: In the set {(1, 8), (2, 8), (5, 8)}, list the dependent variables (y-values).
sample_items.distractor_logic: The y-values are all 8; the independent values are 1, 2, 5.

redirect_script.stop: Which number do you choose -- the first or the second?
redirect_script.prompt: The independent variable is the input: the x, the FIRST number in the pair, the one you control. The dependent (output) is the y, the second number. Point to the first number and say 'input.'
redirect_script.praise: You picked the x-value as the input -- that's the independent variable.

vocabulary.definition: The input; the x-value; the quantity you choose or change.
The output; the y-value; the quantity that responds to the input.
The value fed into a relation -- the x.
The value a relation produces -- the y.

worked_example_script.text: Which number in each pair is the input you control? What is it called?
The first number is the input: 4, 6, 8 are the independent variables. The second, 9, 2, 5, are the dependent variables.
If a student lists 9, 2, 5 as independent, ask 'which one did you choose first, and which one responded?'
Your turn: in {(1, 7), (3, 7)}, name the independent and dependent variables.

practice_problems.stem: In the ordered pair (5, 12), which value is the independent variable?
practice_problems.answer: 5 (the x-value)

practice_problems.stem: Is the input the independent variable or the dependent variable?
practice_problems.answer: The independent variable.

practice_problems.stem: In the set {(3, -5), (-2, 4), (7, 1)}, which numbers are independent variables?
practice_problems.notes: First coordinate of each pair; baits reading the y-values.

practice_problems.stem: A chart pairs each student's name with their test score. Which is the dependent variable?
practice_problems.answer: The test score (it depends on / responds to the student).
practice_problems.notes: Context version; score is the output.

practice_problems.stem: Dana labeled the variables in a set of ordered pairs. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Dana wrote: 'The independent variables are 9, 6, and 1.'
practice_problems.answer: Dana used the second number (the y / output) as the independent variable. The independent variables are the x-values -- the FIRST number in each pair: 2, 4, and 8. The 9, 6, and 1 are the dependent variables.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: swapping independent and dependent.

practice_problems.stem: In {(1, 8), (2, 8), (5, 8)}, list the dependent variables.
practice_problems.answer: 8, 8, 8 (the y-values).
practice_problems.notes: Outputs can repeat; still the second coordinate.

practice_problems.stem: Write a set of three ordered pairs whose independent variables are 2, 4, and 6.
practice_problems.answer: Any set with those x-values first, e.g. {(2, 5), (4, 5), (6, 9)}.

practice_problems.stem: A friend says 'the dependent variable is whatever number is bigger.' Explain why that is wrong.
practice_problems.answer: The dependent variable is the OUTPUT (the y, the second number), no matter its size. In (3, 1) the dependent variable is 1 even though it is smaller than 3.

activities.title: Input or Output?
materials: Card set of 12 quantities from paired contexts (hours/pay, day/temperature, etc.)
activities.instructions:
1. Read each context card (like 'hours worked -> pay earned').
2. Sort the two quantities into 'Independent (input)' and 'Dependent (output).'
3. For each pair, say the sentence '___ depends on ___' out loud to check.
4. Debrief: which word or arrow tells you which quantity is the input?

activities.title: First Means Input
activities.instructions:
1. Read Dana's claim that the independent variables of {(2, 9), (4, 6), (8, 1)} are 9, 6, 1.
2. Underline the FIRST number in each pair.
3. Write the correct independent variables and the correct dependent variables.
4. Write a rule: which slot is always the input?

content.worked_problem: Set {(2, 9), (4, 6), (8, 1)}. Dana said the independent variables are 9, 6, 1.
content.error_step: Dana read the second number (the output) as the independent variable.
content.why: The independent variable is the input -- the first number: 2, 4, 8. The 9, 6, 1 are the outputs.

strategy_links.why: Swapping input and output is a precise, high-frequency error that a find-and-fix names and corrects cleanly.
Think-pair-share on 'which quantity depends on which' surfaces the input/output relationship for discussion.
Choral response of 'x is the input, y is the output' builds the automatic association this skill needs.

questioning_prompts: Which number in the pair is the one you choose or control?
Say the sentence: '___ depends on ___.' Which is the dependent variable?
Is the independent variable the first coordinate or the second?
Can an output be smaller than its input and still be the output?
Point to the x-values. Are those inputs or outputs?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student names the y-value (output) as the independent variable.
misconception_redirects.say: The independent variable is the input: the x, the FIRST number in the pair, the one you control. The dependent (output) is the y, the second number. Point to the first number and say 'input.'
misconception_redirects.praise: You picked the x-value as the input -- that's the independent variable.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student decides the dependent variable by which number is larger.
misconception_redirects.say: Role comes from position, not size. The second number is the output even when it is smaller. Read the slot, not the value.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the position in the pair, not the size, to name the variable.

quick_checks.prompt: In (9, 4), which value is the independent variable?
quick_checks.look_for: 9 (the x). An answer of 4 diagnoses the swap.

quick_checks.prompt: A table pairs 'minutes' with 'liters filled.' Which is dependent?
quick_checks.look_for: Liters filled (it responds). Naming minutes means the student reversed input and output.

sentence_starters: The independent variable is ___ because it is the input (the x).
The dependent variable is ___ because it responds to the input.

worked_solution.stem: In the set {(4, 9), (6, 2), (8, 5)}, name the independent and dependent variables.

steps.annotation: The first number is the input, the second is the output.
The first coordinate of each pair -- the independent variables.
The second coordinate of each pair -- the dependent variables.
Input values first, output values second.

faded_example.stem: In the set {(1, 7), (3, 2), (5, 8)}, name the independent and dependent variables.

steps.annotation: First number = input, second = output.
Read the first coordinate of each pair.
List the y-values -- the dependent variables.
State which set is independent and which is dependent.

skills.name: State the definition of a function: each input has exactly one output
skills.i_do_script: A function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output -- each x-value has exactly one y-value. Say it as a one-way promise: every input points to a single output. Watch the trap: the reverse, 'every OUTPUT has exactly one input,' is NOT the definition. A function is allowed to send different inputs to the same output; it just can't send one input to two different outputs. So the correct definitions are 'every x has exactly one y' and 'every independent variable has exactly one dependent variable.'

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the definition -- states that each output has exactly one input
canonical_error.example: Chooses 'every y-value has exactly one x-value' as the definition of a function
canonical_error.why: The rule is one-directional: each INPUT maps to exactly one output. A function may send different inputs to the same output, so the restriction lives on the inputs, not the outputs.

skills.item_template: A set of statements about functions. Student selects the correct definition(s). Multiple choice / multi-select.

sample_items.stem: Which statement best describes a function?
sample_items.answer: Every input has exactly one output.
choices: Every input has exactly one output.
Every output has exactly one input.
All inputs and outputs are different numbers.
Any set of ordered pairs is a function.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The definition is one-directional: each input -> one output. 'Every output has one input' reverses it.

sample_items.stem: Which description correctly defines a function?
sample_items.answer: Every independent variable has exactly one dependent variable.
choices: Every independent variable has exactly one dependent variable.
Every dependent variable has exactly one independent variable.
The inputs must all be different from the outputs.
The graph must be a straight line.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Matches the spec's correct answers a and d; the reversed and 'line' options are distractors.

sample_items.stem: True or false: a function can send the same input to two different outputs.
sample_items.answer: False
sample_items.distractor_logic: One input to two outputs violates the definition, so the statement is false.

sample_items.stem: A function assigns to each input exactly how many outputs?
sample_items.answer: Exactly one
choices: As many as there are inputs
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Exactly one' is the definition; 'at least one' would allow multiple outputs.

redirect_script.stop: Which way does the promise go -- input to output, or output to input?
redirect_script.prompt: A function promises each INPUT exactly one output. Read your statement: does it start with the input (the x)? Different inputs may share an output, but one input can't have two.
redirect_script.praise: You stated it input-first: each input gets exactly one output. That's the definition.

vocabulary.definition: A rule that assigns to each input exactly one output.
One and only one -- not zero, not two.
Any set of ordered pairs; a function is a special relation.

worked_example_script.text: Write two statements: 'every x has one y' and 'every y has one x.'
Which one is the definition of a function? Which direction does it go?
The definition is 'every x has exactly one y' -- input to output. 'Every y has one x' is the reverse and is NOT required.
If a student picks the reverse, ask 'can two different inputs share an output? Yes -- so the rule must be about inputs.'
Your turn: finish the sentence 'A function assigns each input exactly ___ output.'

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: A function assigns each input exactly ___ output.
practice_problems.answer: one

practice_problems.stem: In a function, which is restricted to one partner -- the input or the output?
practice_problems.answer: The input (each input has exactly one output).

practice_problems.stem: Which is the correct definition: 'every x-value has exactly one y-value' or 'every y-value has exactly one x-value'?
practice_problems.answer: Every x-value has exactly one y-value.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: a function may assign the same output to two different inputs.
practice_problems.answer: True -- repeated outputs are allowed; only repeated inputs with different outputs are not.
practice_problems.notes: The allowed direction; core to the standard.

practice_problems.stem: Reed defined a function. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Reed wrote: 'A relation is a function when every output has exactly one input.'
practice_problems.answer: Reed reversed the definition. A function requires every INPUT to have exactly one output (every x has one y). Different inputs are allowed to share an output, so the restriction is on inputs, not outputs.

practice_problems.stem: Select all that define a function: (a) every input has one output; (b) every output has one input; (c) every independent variable has one dependent variable.
practice_problems.answer: a and c
practice_problems.notes: Two correct input-first statements; b is the reversal.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why 'a function is just any set of ordered pairs' is wrong.
practice_problems.answer: Every function is a set of ordered pairs, but not every set of ordered pairs is a function -- only those where each input has exactly one output. {(2, 5), (2, 9)} is a set of ordered pairs but not a function.

practice_problems.stem: Write the definition of a function in your own words, then give one example of what a function is NOT allowed to do.
practice_problems.answer: A function gives each input exactly one output. It is not allowed to send one input (x) to two different outputs (y), like x = 2 going to both 5 and 9.

activities.title: Definition or Not?
materials: Statement cards, some true definitions of a function and some near-miss reversals
activities.instructions:
1. Sort each statement into 'Defines a function' or 'Does NOT define a function.'
2. For every 'does not' card, say why: is it reversed, is it about size, or is it too broad?
3. Star the one error that shows up most (the reversed one).
4. Debrief: which direction does a function's promise go?

cards.text: Every input has exactly one output.
Every x-value has exactly one y-value.
Every independent variable has one dependent variable.
Every output has exactly one input.
Every dependent variable has one independent variable.
All inputs and outputs must be different numbers.
Any set of ordered pairs is a function.

activities.title: Which Way Does It Go?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Reed's definition: 'a function is when every output has exactly one input.'
2. Find a function that breaks Reed's version but is still a real function -- try {(1, 5), (2, 5)}.
3. Rewrite the definition the correct way.
4. Write one sentence on why the rule is about inputs, not outputs.

content.worked_problem: Reed wrote: 'A function is when every output has exactly one input.'
content.error_step: Reed reversed the direction of the definition.
content.why: A function requires each input to have one output. {(1, 5), (2, 5)} sends two inputs to the same output 5 and is still a function, so the rule can't be about outputs.

strategy_links.why: The reversed definition is a precise, nameable error that find-and-fix targets directly.
Think-pair-share on 'input to output or output to input?' forces students to defend the direction of the definition.
A journal entry rewriting the definition in the student's own words consolidates the one-directional rule.

questioning_prompts: Which direction does the definition go -- input to output or the reverse?
Is a function allowed to send two inputs to the same output?
Is a function allowed to send one input to two outputs?
Does 'exactly one' mean the same as 'at least one'?
Is every set of ordered pairs a function? Why or why not?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student states that each output has exactly one input.
misconception_redirects.say: A function promises each INPUT exactly one output. Read your statement: does it start with the input (the x)? Different inputs may share an output, but one input can't have two.
misconception_redirects.praise: You stated it input-first: each input gets exactly one output. That's the definition.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says inputs and outputs must all be different numbers.
misconception_redirects.say: A function has no rule that inputs and outputs differ -- (3, 3) is fine. The only rule is one output per input.
misconception_redirects.praise: You focused on the one-output-per-input rule instead of the numbers being different.

quick_checks.prompt: Finish: 'A function assigns each input exactly ___ output.'
quick_checks.look_for: one. 'At least one' or 'two' misses 'exactly one.'

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: 'every output has exactly one input' defines a function.
quick_checks.look_for: False. A 'true' answer diagnoses the reversed definition.

sentence_starters: A function assigns each input exactly ___ output.
This statement is / is not the definition because it goes from ___ to ___.

worked_solution.stem: Which statement is the definition of a function: (a) every x-value has exactly one y-value, or (b) every y-value has exactly one x-value?

steps.math: a function assigns each INPUT one output
steps.annotation: The promise starts with the input (x).

steps.math: (a) every x has exactly one y -> input to output
steps.annotation: Matches the definition.

steps.math: (b) every y has one x -> output to input
steps.annotation: This is the reverse; not required for a function.
Different inputs may share an output, so the rule is about inputs.

faded_example.stem: Select the correct definition: (a) every input has exactly one output; (b) every output has exactly one input; (c) all inputs differ from all outputs.

steps.math: a function assigns each input one output
steps.annotation: State the one-directional rule.
Compare (a) to the rule.
Explain why (b) is the reverse and is wrong.
Explain why (c) is not part of the definition.

skills.name: Determine whether a set of ordered pairs is a function
skills.i_do_script: To decide if a set of ordered pairs is a function, I hunt for a REPEATED x-value that is paired with DIFFERENT y-values. If I find one, it is not a function; if every x-value is different (or a repeat has the same y), it is a function. Watch {(2, 5), (3, 7), (2, 9), (4, 5)}: x = 2 shows up twice, once with y = 5 and once with y = 9 -- two different outputs for one input, so this is NOT a function. Notice y = 5 also repeats (with x = 2 and x = 4), but repeated OUTPUTS are fine; only a repeated input with different outputs breaks it.

canonical_error.pattern: Disqualifies a relation because a y-value (output) repeats, instead of checking for a repeated x with different y
canonical_error.example: Calls {(2, 3), (4, 3), (6, 3)} 'not a function' because the output 3 repeats, when every input is different so it IS a function
canonical_error.why: The student applies the rule to outputs instead of inputs. Repeated outputs are allowed; only a repeated INPUT paired with two different outputs violates the definition.

skills.item_template: A set of ordered pairs. Student decides function / not a function and explains. MC / multi-part.

sample_items.stem: Does the set {(2, 5), (3, 7), (2, 9), (4, 5)} represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. x = 2 is paired with both 5 and 9 -- one input, two different outputs.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Repeated input (2) with different outputs breaks it; the repeated output 5 does NOT.

sample_items.stem: Does the set {(1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12)} represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Every x-value is different, so each input has exactly one output.
sample_items.distractor_logic: All inputs unique -> function.

sample_items.stem: Does the set {(-2, 4), (0, 4), (3, 4), (5, 4)} represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. The inputs -2, 0, 3, 5 are all different; the repeated output 4 is allowed.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Baits the repeated-output error; inputs are unique so it is a function.

sample_items.stem: Does the set {(4, 1), (5, 2), (4, 7), (6, 3)} represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. x = 4 is paired with both 1 and 7 -- two outputs for one input.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Repeated input 4 with different outputs -> not a function.

redirect_script.stop: Are you checking the x's or the y's?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the x-values only. Look for the SAME x appearing with two DIFFERENT y's -- that's the only thing that breaks a function. A repeated y by itself is fine.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the inputs for a repeat with different outputs -- that's the real test.

vocabulary.definition: The same x-value appearing in more than one ordered pair.
A set where no x-value is paired with two different y-values.

worked_example_script.text: Which x-value repeats? Do its y-values match or differ?
x = 1 appears twice, with y = 4 and y = 9 -- different outputs. So this is NOT a function.
If a student says 'not a function' because a y repeats, ask 'is it a repeated INPUT with different outputs?'
Your turn: is {(2, 5), (4, 5), (6, 5)} a function?

practice_problems.answer: Yes -- every input is different.

practice_problems.stem: Is {(2, 5), (2, 8)} a function?
practice_problems.answer: No -- input 2 has two different outputs (5 and 8).

practice_problems.stem: Is {(2, 5), (3, 7), (2, 9), (4, 5)} a function? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- x = 2 maps to 5 and 9.
practice_problems.notes: Repeated input with different outputs; the repeated output 5 is a distractor.

practice_problems.stem: Is {(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4)} a function? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- inputs 1, 2, 3 are all different; the repeated output 4 is allowed.

practice_problems.stem: Mia decided whether a set is a function. Find and fix the mistake.

skills.name: Determine whether a table or mapping represents a function
skills.i_do_script: A table or mapping is a function by the same test as ordered pairs: read the input (x) column and look for a repeated input tied to different outputs. Watch a table with x = 1, 2, 3, 5 and y = 4, 4, 4, 4: every x is different, so even though the outputs are all 4, each input has exactly one output -- it IS a function. Now a table with x = 2, 4, 2, 6 and y = 5, 7, 8, 9: x = 2 appears twice with 5 and 8, two outputs for one input, so it is NOT a function. In a mapping, a function has exactly one arrow leaving each input.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges the table by the OUTPUT column -- calls repeated y-values a non-function (or requires all outputs to differ)
canonical_error.example: Says a table with x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 5, 5, 8 is 'not a function' because two outputs are 5, when every input is different so it IS a function
canonical_error.why: The student scans the wrong column. A table is a function when each INPUT appears with one output; repeated outputs across different inputs are allowed.

skills.name: Determine whether a graph is a function using the vertical line test
skills.i_do_script: Because the graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs (x, y), testing a graph is just checking inputs visually: the VERTICAL line test. If any vertical line (a line straight up and down at a single x-value) touches the graph in more than one point, that x-value has two outputs, so it is NOT a function. Watch a straight slanted line like y = 2x: every vertical line crosses it exactly once, so it IS a function. A circle fails: a vertical line through the middle hits it at two points. Careful -- it is the VERTICAL line you slide across, not a horizontal one.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses a horizontal line test (or checks for repeated y-values) instead of the vertical line test
canonical_error.example: Calls a horizontal line y = 3, or an upward U-shaped parabola, 'not a function' because many x-values share the same y-value
canonical_error.why: The student tests outputs instead of inputs. The rule is about each input having one output, so the line you slide must be VERTICAL (one x at a time); repeated y-values do not matter.

skills.item_template: A graph described as plotted points or as a named curve. Student applies the vertical line test. MC / short response. (Figures are described in text so the item is render-safe.)

sample_items.stem: A graph consists of the plotted points (1, 2), (2, 4), (1, 5), and (3, 1). Does the graph represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. A vertical line at x = 1 passes through both (1, 2) and (1, 5), so x = 1 has two outputs.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Two points share x = 1 -> vertical line hits twice -> not a function.

sample_items.stem: A graph is a straight slanted line rising to the right (like the line y = 2x). Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Every vertical line crosses the slanted line exactly once, so each x has one y.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Passes the vertical line test.

sample_items.stem: A graph is a circle. Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. A vertical line through the middle of the circle crosses it at two points, so one x has two y-values.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Fails the vertical line test.

sample_items.stem: A graph is a single vertical line at x = 4. Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. The input x = 4 is paired with every y-value on the line, so it has more than one output.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A vertical line is the extreme failure: one x, infinitely many y. Baits confusing 'vertical line test' with 'the graph is a vertical line.'

sample_items.stem: A graph is a U-shaped parabola opening upward (like y = x squared). Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Every vertical line crosses the parabola exactly once, so each x has one y (even though outputs repeat on the two sides).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Baits the horizontal-line/repeated-output error; it passes the vertical line test.

redirect_script.stop: Which way does your test line go -- up-and-down or side-to-side?
redirect_script.prompt: Slide a VERTICAL line (straight up and down) across the graph. If it ever touches two points at once, it is not a function. A horizontal line does not test this -- repeated y-values are allowed.
redirect_script.praise: You used a vertical line and checked for two points at one x -- that's the function test.

vocabulary.definition: If any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, the graph is not a function.
A straight up-and-down line at a single x-value.
An unbroken curve or line, as opposed to separate plotted points.

worked_example_script.text: Describe two graphs: a slanted line, and a set of points including (2, 1) and (2, 5).
Slide a vertical line across each. Does it ever hit two points at once?
The slanted line: every vertical line hits once -> function. The points: a vertical line at x = 2 hits (2, 1) and (2, 5) -> not a function.
If a student slides a horizontal line, ask 'does the rule limit outputs per input, or inputs per output?'
Your turn: does a horizontal line y = 3 pass the vertical line test?

practice_problems.answer: Priya used a horizontal line. The correct test is the VERTICAL line test: any vertical line crosses y = 3 exactly once, so each x has one output. It IS a function. Repeated y-values are allowed.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: horizontal line test / repeated outputs.

practice_problems.stem: A graph is a single vertical line at x = 4. Is it a function? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- x = 4 is paired with every y on the line, so it has many outputs.

practice_problems.stem: A sideways U-shaped parabola opens to the RIGHT (like x = y squared). Is it a function? Explain using the vertical line test.
practice_problems.answer: No -- a vertical line to the right of the vertex crosses it at two points (one above and one below the x-axis), so one x has two y-values.
practice_problems.notes: Sideways parabola fails; contrast with the upward parabola.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why an upward parabola IS a function but a circle is NOT, even though both are curves with repeated y-values.
practice_problems.answer: The vertical line test decides it: every vertical line hits the upward parabola once, but a vertical line through a circle hits it twice. Repeated y-values are fine; two points at one x are not.

skills.name: Justify whether a real-world relation is a function and critique reasoning
skills.i_do_script: In a real-world relation I first decide which quantity is the input (independent variable) and which is the output (dependent variable), then apply the same test: does any input have two different outputs? Watch the kayak table -- hours rented paired with cost, where cost stays at 20 after hour 4. A classmate says it is not a function because the cost 20 repeats. But hours is the INPUT and each hour appears once, so each input has one cost. The repeated OUTPUT does not matter -- it IS a function. I justify with the definition, and I check whether a critique is judging by the input or the output.

canonical_error.pattern: In a context, judges function-status by whether the OUTPUT values repeat rather than the inputs
canonical_error.example: Says the kayak cost table {(1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15), (4, 20), (5, 20), (6, 20)} is not a function because the cost 20 repeats, when each hour (input) is unique so it IS a function
canonical_error.why: The student picks the wrong quantity as the one that must be unique. Function-status depends on each INPUT having one output; repeated real-world outputs (same price, same height) are allowed.

skills.item_template: A real-world relation as a table or story, sometimes with a classmate's claim. Student decides, justifies, or critiques. Multi-part.

sample_items.stem: A machine dispenses water by seconds: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8) [seconds, liters]. Is this a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Each number of seconds (input) gives exactly one amount of water, so it is a function.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Every input appears once -> function.

sample_items.stem: A store records (price, shirt color): $10 -> red, $10 -> blue, $15 -> green. Is 'price -> color' a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. The price $10 (input) is paired with two different colors (red and blue), so one input has two outputs.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Repeated input $10 with different outputs -> not a function.

sample_items.stem: A kayak rents by the hour; after hour 4 the price stays at $20. Table [hours, cost]: (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15), (4, 20), (5, 20), (6, 20). A classmate says it is NOT a function because the cost 20 repeats. Is the classmate correct? Explain.
sample_items.answer: The classmate is incorrect. Hours is the input and each hour appears once, so each input has one cost -- it IS a function. The repeated output ($20) is allowed.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Critique targets the repeated-output error; unique inputs make it a function.

sample_items.stem: A girl records her height each birthday, ages 4 to 9 [age, height]: (4, 40), (5, 43), (6, 45), (7, 48), (8, 50), (9, 53). Is this relation a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Each age (input) has exactly one height, so it is a function.
sample_items.distractor_logic: All inputs (ages) unique -> function.

redirect_script.praise: You named the input and tested it -- not the repeated output. That's the real justification.

practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: repeated output as disqualifying, plus swapped variables (matches the spec's kayak item).

practice_problems.stem: A vending machine gives water by seconds: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8). Is 'seconds -> liters' a function? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- each number of seconds gives exactly one amount of water.

practice_problems.stem: Describe a real-world relation that is NOT a function, and explain which input has two outputs.
practice_problems.answer: Answers vary, e.g. 'a person's phone number -> the people who share it': one number (input) can reach a whole household (many outputs). The input repeats with different outputs.

practice_problems.stem: Two students disagree about a 'day -> high temperature' table where two days both hit 71 degrees. One says it is a function, one says it is not. Who is right and why?
practice_problems.answer: The one who says it IS a function is right. Day is the input and each day appears once; the repeated output (71 degrees) does not matter.

activities.title: Real-World: Function or Not?
materials: Context cards (each names an input, an output, and whether an input or an output repeats)
activities.instructions:
1. For each card, underline the INPUT (independent variable).
2. Sort into 'Function' or 'Not a function' by checking only whether an input repeats with two different outputs.
3. Flag any card where only the OUTPUT repeats -- those are still functions.
4. Debrief: which real-world quantity has to be unique for a function?

activities.title: Critique the Boater
materials: Slip with the boater's claim about the kayak table
activities.instructions:
1. Read the boater's claim that the kayak table is not a function because the costs are 'the independent variable and not all unique.'
2. Label the real independent and dependent variables.
3. Decide whether the table is a function and justify with the definition.
4. Write one sentence telling the boater exactly where the reasoning went wrong.

content.worked_problem: Kayak table (hours, cost): (1,5),(2,10),(3,15),(4,20),(5,20),(6,20). Boater: 'Not a function -- costs are the independent variable and are not all unique.'
content.error_step: The boater called cost the independent variable and judged by repeated outputs.
content.why: Hours is the input and each hour is unique, so each input has one cost -- it is a function. The repeated cost $20 is an allowed repeated output.

strategy_links.why: Critiquing the boater's claim is a direct find-and-fix on the repeated-output misconception in context.
Think-pair-share on 'who is right and why' pushes students to justify with the definition and challenge flawed reasoning.
A written justification in a math journal builds the explanation muscle this above-grade skill demands.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity in the story is the input? Which is the output?
Does any input value repeat with two different outputs?
Is a repeated price, height, or cost enough to break the function?
Is the classmate judging by the input or the output?
State the definition of a function to justify your answer.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student judges a real-world relation by whether the output values repeat.
misconception_redirects.say: Name the input (the independent variable) first. Then check ONLY whether an input repeats with two different outputs. A repeated price, height, or cost by itself does not break the function.
misconception_redirects.praise: You named the input and tested it -- not the repeated output. That's the real justification.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the independent and dependent variables in the story.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask 'which quantity depends on which?' The one you set or control is the input; the one that responds is the output.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the input to the quantity you control -- now the test lines up.

quick_checks.prompt: A 'day -> temperature' table has two days at 71 degrees. Function?
quick_checks.look_for: Yes -- days are unique inputs. A 'no' diagnoses the repeated-output error.

quick_checks.prompt: A 'price -> color' relation has $10 -> red and $10 -> blue. Function?
quick_checks.look_for: No -- input $10 has two outputs. A 'yes' means the repeated input was missed.

sentence_starters: The input here is ___, so I check whether ___ repeats with two outputs.
The classmate is right / wrong because a repeated ___ ...

worked_solution.stem: A student records the temperature each hour from noon: (12, 70), (1, 72), (2, 75), (3, 74), (4, 71) [hour, degrees]. Is this relation a function?

steps.annotation: Name the independent and dependent variables.
Check the inputs for a repeat.

steps.math: each hour has exactly one temperature
steps.annotation: No input maps to two outputs.
It satisfies the definition of a function.

faded_example.stem: A pizza shop records (order number, topping): (1, pepperoni), (2, mushroom), (1, sausage). Is 'order number -> topping' a function?
faded_example.answer: No -- it is not a function.

steps.annotation: Name the input and output.
Check the inputs for a repeat.
State the two toppings order 1 is paired with.
Decide function or not, and justify.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (is a set of ordered pairs a function?) -- the core grade-level determination and where the repeated-output misconception lives. If they pass, move through S4 (tables/mappings) and S5 (graphs, vertical line test). If they fail, drop to S2 to check the definition and S1 to check independent vs dependent variables. S6 (justify and critique a real-world relation) branches off as the above-grade synthesis.
